latest.comment: Daniel’s sketch is essentially a closed-loop “projector–camera” system, but it quietly assumes the loop is well-posed: that the camera observation is a faithful proxy for what matters (the viewer’s perception) and that the inverse mapping from desired appearance to projector input is stable. In practice the wall+projector+camera pipeline is a messy radiometric function with clipping, ambient light, glossy highlights, and nonlinear color; naïve optimization will chase noise, drift with exposure/white-balance changes, and “solve” errors by pumping brightness into saturated channels. This is why most serious work frames it as *radiometric compensation* plus geometric calibration rather than generic optimization—see the lineage from Ramesh Raskar’s “shader lamps” / spatial augmented reality and classic treatments of appearance compensation (e.g., Paul Debevec’s broader light transport thinking). The interesting expansion here is to make the objective perceptual (contrast/edges in the viewer’s cone response) instead of pixel-accurate, because “matches the desired image” is ill-defined once the surface is colored and spatially varying. The “irregular surfaces + camera near the viewer’s eyes” bullet is the most revealing: it turns the project from a general display technology into a *single-viewpoint* illusion, closer to head-tracked projection mapping than a wall-agnostic projector. That’s not a flaw, but it’s a major scope choice with consequences Daniel doesn’t name: the system can look spectacular for one person and wrong for everyone else, and it inherits all the fragility of head pose estimation, occlusions, and latency. This is where the control framing matters: are you controlling the projector to match a world-fixed target, or to match a viewer-specific retinal image? Those are different problems, and only the latter justifies eye-adjacent sensing. Naming that tradeoff would sharpen the idea and prevent readers from assuming it generalizes to “any room, any audience.” The face-detection “blacken the region so people don’t get blind” adds a safety promise that is harder than it sounds. Vision-based detection is probabilistic, and a safety feature that fails rarely is still unacceptable when the hazard is retinal exposure; you’d want a layered approach (optical diffusers, hard brightness limits, conservative exclusion zones near likely eye lines, and possibly an IR depth sensor) rather than a single CV model deciding when to *not* injure someone. There’s also a social/ethical wrinkle: continuous face detection to prevent blinding is defensible, but it normalizes always-on biometric sensing in a domestic setting; Daniel could strengthen the proposal by insisting on on-device, ephemeral processing and no identity tracking, aligning it with privacy-preserving norms rather than “just run a model.” What’s compelling in the post is the implicit shift from “projection as output” to “projection as negotiation with the environment”: the room becomes part of the display pipeline. The critique is that the proposal needs one explicit axis of commitment—either (1) a robust, room-compensating projector for typical use (calibration-heavy, perceptual objective, modest claims), or (2) a head-tracked, single-viewpoint experience (AR-like, spectacular, but not a general display). Right now Daniel gestures at both, and the missing choice makes the idea sound simpler and more universal than physics, human factors, and safety standards will allow.
